map.A data & statistics mystery in five chap: A data & statistics mystery in five chapters, with six reader gates. Solve the math to move the story.
map.Pattern distortion detected, crew. This: Pattern distortion found, crew. This one smells like… paperwork.
map.Previously: on a rained-out field day, f: Before: on a rainy field day, four sixth graders opened Ada Vex's sealed journal in the old Vexhall Observatory. They woke VEX, a piece of her Pattern Engine. Now the city's patterns are their problem.
map.Founders Festival, day six. Rosa's churr: Founders Festival, day six. Rosa's churros are the best thing in Axiom City—
map.—and the census office says nobody visit: —and the census office says nobody visits my stall. Nobody? Look at this line!
map.Distortion source located: the festival: Distortion source found: the festival census report. The data has been… bent. Crew, check it.
map.The census office window. A very tall cl: The census office window. A very tall clipboard. A very proud clerk.
map.The census is official. Data is data, ch: The census is official. Data is data, children. Numbers don't lie.
map.Data starts with questions, Mr. Pimm. Ba: Data starts with questions, Mr. Pimm. Bad questions make bent data. What did yours ask?
map.Definition loaded: a statistical questio: Definition loaded: a statistical question expects answers that VARY. Different people give different answers. A question with one answer is just a fact.
map.A statistical question anticipates varie: A statistical question expects many different answers. "How many minutes do visitors stay?" has many answers. "What time does the festival open?" has exactly one.
map.Reader — you're our fifth crew member. T: Reader, you're our fifth crew member. Tag Pimm's census questions!
map.Pimm's census form, four questions. Tag: Pimm's census form has four questions. Tag each one: STATISTICAL (answers vary) or ONE ANSWER (a single fact).
map.Conceptual: a statistical question antic: Conceptual: a statistical question expects VARIETY. Ask it to 100 visitors and you get many different answers. A fact question has one answer no matter who you ask.
map.Procedural: test each question — 'Would: Procedural: test each question. 'Would two visitors give two different answers?' Minutes stayed and money spent change from person to person. Opening time and stall count do not.
map.Behind Rosa's stall. The logbook smells: Behind Rosa's stall. The logbook smells like cinnamon.
map.\"Nobody,\" huh? Line these up smallest: "Nobody," huh? Put these in order, smallest to largest. The median is the middle value. It shows Rosa's typical day.
map.Median protocol: ORDER the data first. O: Median plan: ORDER the data first. Odd count: one exact middle. Even count: average the two middle values. Wild days barely move it.
map.The median is the middle value of an ord: The median is the middle value of a data set in order. It is a measure of center. Extreme values barely move it.
map.Order Rosa's five days and find her real: Order Rosa's five days. Find her real "typical day," reader.
map.Rosa's logbook, five festival days: 51,: Rosa's logbook, five festival days: 51, 38, 60, 45, 42 visitors. Find the median, her typical day.
map.Conceptual: the median is the middle of: Conceptual: the median is the middle of the list IN ORDER. Half the days are below it. Half are above it. (If the count were even, you would average the TWO middle values.)
map.Procedural: write the five numbers small: Procedural: write the five numbers from smallest to largest: 38, 42, …, …, 60. Cross off one number from each end, twice. The one left is the median.
map.Side quest complete: I tallied Rosa's vi: Side quest done: I counted Rosa's visitors in every half-hour block, all day. Sixteen data points. Raw loot.
map.Raw numbers are mush. I could build that: Raw numbers are a mess. I could build that. Stack them into bars. A histogram.
map.Histogram schema: sort data into equal i: Histogram plan: sort data into equal intervals (bins). Each bar's height = the frequency. That is how many values land in that bin. Bars touch. No gaps.
map.A histogram shows how often data falls i: A histogram shows how often data falls in each interval. Height = frequency. The bars touch because the intervals touch.
map.Hand me the bar heights, reader — let's: Give me the bar heights, reader. Let's stack Dev's tally into the truth!
map.Dev's tally — visitors in each of 16 hal:
Dev's tally: visitors in each of 16 half-hour blocks:
12 · 3 · 25 · 14 · 7 · 18 · 22 · 11 · 9 · 27 · 16 · 5 · 13 · 21 · 19 · 20
Count how many blocks land in each bin. Then set the three bar heights.
map.Conceptual: each bar's height is a FREQU: Conceptual: each bar's height is a FREQUENCY. It is how many of the 16 numbers fall inside that interval. Every number lands in exactly one bin.
map.Procedural: go number by number and tick: Procedural: go number by number and tick a bin: 12→(10–19), 3→(0–9), 25→(20–29)… Your three counts must add up to 16.
map.City Hall, Hall of Charts. The official: City Hall, Hall of Charts. The official festival box plot hangs… crooked.
map.A box plot with no numbers is a lock wit: A box plot with no numbers is a lock with no key. Lucky for us, we logged seven checkpoint counts ourselves: 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 30, 35.
Boss-key time: min, Q1, median, Q3, max. The five-number summary.
map.A box plot draws the five-number summary: A box plot draws the five-number summary. The box runs Q1 → Q3 with the median inside. Whiskers reach min and max. IQR = Q3 − Q1. It is the spread of the middle half.
map.Quartiles split ordered data into four e: Quartiles split data in order into four equal parts. The interquartile range (IQR) shows how spread out the middle half is.
map.Cut the five-number key, reader — then w: Cut the five-number key, reader. Then we can read any box plot they hang.
map.The crew's seven checkpoint counts, alre: The crew's seven checkpoint counts, already in order: 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 30, 35. Cut the key: find Q1, the median, Q3, and the IQR. (Min = 12 and max = 35 are free.)
map.Conceptual: the median splits the data i: Conceptual: the median splits the data in half. Q1 is the median of the LOWER half. Q3 is the median of the UPPER half. IQR = Q3 − Q1, the width of the box.
map.Procedural: median = 4th of 7 values. Lo: Procedural: median = 4th of 7 values. The lower half is the three values below it. Find their middle. The upper half is the three above it. Find their middle. Then subtract.
map.Rosa's storeroom, dawn. The hearing is a: Rosa's storeroom, dawn. The hearing is at noon.
map.Five days of churro batches: 14, 9, 16,: Five days of churro batches: 14, 9, 16, 13, 8. If every day got a fair share, how tall is each stack?
map.That fair share has a name: the mean. To: That fair share has a name: the mean. Add everything up. Divide by the number of days.
map.The mean = sum ÷ count. It levels every: The mean = sum ÷ count. It levels every stack to the same height. It is the "fair share" measure of center.
map.Level the stacks, reader — the hearing w: Level the stacks, reader. The hearing won't wait!
map.Two levelings before the hearing: ① Chur:
Two levelings before the hearing:
① Churro batches over 5 days: 14, 9, 16, 13, 8. Find the mean.
② The cider barrel poured 94.5 L over 7 days. Find the mean liters per day (decimal division!).
map.Conceptual: the mean is the fair share —: Conceptual: the mean is the fair share. Pour every day's count into one pot. Then split the pot equally among the days.
map.Procedural: ① add the five numbers, divi: Procedural: ① add the five numbers, divide by 5. ② divide 94.5 by 7. Or split it: 94.5 = 70 + 24.5, and each part divides by 7 evenly.
map.City Hall hearing room, 12:00 sharp. Cle: City Hall hearing room, 12:00 sharp. Clerk Pimm has a very big folder.
map.Her log \"averages\" 65.4 visitors — yet: Her log "averages" 65.4 visitors. But I never counted more than 50 at her stall! The log is crooked. Permit DENIED.
map.Or your summary is crooked, Mr. Pimm. On: Or your summary is crooked, Mr. Pimm. One number in that week is screaming. Reader, run both measures.
map.An outlier is a value far from the rest: An outlier is a value far from the rest of the data. It pulls the mean toward it. But the median barely moves. Boss Gate: find both, then choose the honest one.
map.BOSS GATE. Four locks. One outlier. Rosa: BOSS GATE. Four locks. One outlier. Rosa's permit is at stake. (No pressure. Some pressure.)
map.Rosa's full week: 41, 44, 45, 47, 150 (1: Rosa's full week: 41, 44, 45, 47, 150 (150 = parade day, when every stall spiked). Pimm waves the "average." Four locks to save the permit:
map.Which measure honestly represents Rosa's: Which measure honestly shows Rosa's typical day?
map.Conceptual: an outlier drags the MEAN to: Conceptual: an outlier pulls the MEAN toward it like a magnet. But the MEDIAN only cares about position. It barely moves. The honest 'typical day' is the measure the outlier can't bend.
map.Procedural: Lock 1: add all five (watch: Procedural: Lock 1: add all five (watch the 150) and divide by 5. Lock 2: the data is already in order. Take the 3rd value. Locks 3–4: compare your two numbers to the days Rosa really had.
map.Free batch for the audit crew! The media: Free batch for the audit crew! The median saved my stall: 45 honest visitors a day.
map.Pimm's \"crooked log\" was honest data p: Pimm's "crooked log" was honest data with the wrong summary. The council made him issue the whole census again.
map.New distortion. This one moves fast. To: New distortion. This one moves fast. To be continued…
map.Crew captain. Keeps the notebook, asks t: Crew captain. Keeps the notebook, asks the next question. This volume: cracked the five-number key on the crooked chart.
map.Evidence officer. Allergic to \"data is: Evidence officer. Hates "data is data." This volume: won the argument with a clerk using a median.
map.Builder and artist. This volume: stacked: Builder and artist. This volume: stacked sixteen tallies into one strong histogram.
map.Pattern hunter. This volume: a full-day: Pattern hunter. This volume: a full-day tally and one outlier spotted.
map.Churro artist of Founders Festival. Coun: Churro artist of Founders Festival. Counts her visitors by hand, every day. Honest to the last data point.
map.Fragment of Ada Vex's Pattern Engine. Se: Part of Ada Vex's Pattern Engine. Senses distortions. Cannot compute. That's your job.
map.Statistical question.Expects answers tha: Statistical question.Expects answers that vary: "How many minutes do visitors stay?" Not "What time do we open?"
map.Median.Order the data; take the middle (: Median.Put the data in order. Take the middle (or average the two middles). 38 42 45 51 60 → 45.
map.Histogram.Equal intervals, bar height =: Histogram.Equal intervals, bar height = frequency, bars touch. 16 blocks → bins of 4, 7, 5.
map.Box plot & IQR.Five-number summary: min,: Box plot & IQR.Five-number summary: min, Q1, median, Q3, max. IQR = Q3 − Q1 = the spread of the middle half.
map.Mean.Sum ÷ count = the fair share. 60 ch: Mean.Sum ÷ count = the fair share. 60 churro batches ÷ 5 days = 12; 94.5 L ÷ 7 = 13.5.
map.Outlier.A far-off value. It drags the me: Outlier.A value far from the rest. It pulls the mean (45 → 65.4!) but barely moves the median. Choose your measure honestly.
map.\"A single number can hide a whole story: "One number can hide a whole story. Ask the data what varies. Then pick the number that tells the truth." — A.V.
map.completed Volume 2: The Crooked Census a: completed Volume 2: The Crooked Census and proved mastery over statistical questions, median, histograms, box plots, IQR, mean, and outliers.
map.Thank you for auditing with the crew. Vo: Thank you for checking the data. Volume 3 is waiting at the starting line.
map.Different form: 'How tall are Vexhall si: New question: 'How tall are Vexhall sixth graders?' Heights vary student to student, so it is statistical.
map.'How many doors does the observatory hav: 'How many doors does the observatory have?' One fixed count, so it is NOT statistical.
map.The test is variability, not whether the: The test is variability, not if the answer is a number. Both answers are numbers. Only one varies.
map.Your turn — same idea, different numbers: Your turn. Same idea, new numbers:
map.A survey asks 4 questions; 3 of them hav: A survey asks 4 questions. 3 of them have answers that vary. How many are statistical?
map.Different log: 9, 4, 12, 7, 10. Order it: A new log: 9, 4, 12, 7, 10. Put it in order → 4, 7, 9, 10, 12.
map.Cross off ends in pairs: (4,12) gone, (7: Cross off ends in pairs: (4,12) gone, (7,10) gone. Middle is 9.
map.Even-count twist: for 4, 7, 9, 10 there': Even-count twist: 4, 7, 9, 10 has no single middle. Average the two middles: (7+9) ÷ 2 = 8.
map.Tick each value: 0–4 gets 2, 4, 1 → heig: Tick each value: 0–4 gets 2, 4, 1 → height 3. 5–9 gets 7, 6 → height 2. 10–14 gets 11, 13, 12 → height 3.
map.Check the total: 3 + 2 + 3 = 8 values. A: Check the total: 3 + 2 + 3 = 8 values. All the data is counted. No gaps between bars.
map.In that worked tally, how tall is the 10: In that worked tally, how tall is the 10–14 bar?
map.Lower half 2, 4, 6 → Q1 = 4. Upper half: Lower half 2, 4, 6 → Q1 = 4. Upper half 10, 12, 14 → Q3 = 12.
map.IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 12 − 4 = 8. The box woul: IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 12 − 4 = 8. The box would go from 4 to 12 with a line at 8.
map.For that worked data, what is the IQR?: For that worked data, what is the IQR?
map.Different stand: 5, 9, 7, 3 trays over 4: A new stand: 5, 9, 7, 3 trays over 4 days. Total = 5+9+7+3 = 24.
map.Decimal version: 25.5 L ÷ 3 days. 25.5 =: Decimal version: 25.5 L ÷ 3 days. 25.5 = 24 + 1.5 → 8 + 0.5 = 8.5 L per day.
A new stall's week: 10, 12, 14, 100. Mean = 136 ÷ 4 = 34. But NO day was near 34.
map.Median: even count, so average the two m: Median: even count, so average the two middles: (12 + 14) ÷ 2 = 13. That fits the real days.
map.The 100 dragged the mean to 34; the medi: The 100 pulled the mean up to 34. The median stayed at 13. With an outlier, use the median.
map.For that week (10, 12, 14, 100), what is: For that week (10, 12, 14, 100), what is the median?
map.Tag all four questions first — every lin: Tag all four questions first. Every line on the form.
map.Sorted! Two statistical (stay time, spen: Sorted! Two statistical (stay time, spending) and two facts. Pimm's census never asked one statistical question. No wonder it's bent.
map.Ordered: 38, 42, 45, 51, 60 — the middle: In order: 38, 42, 45, 51, 60. The middle is 45. Rosa's typical day is 45 visitors, not 'nobody.'
map.4 + 7 + 5 = all 16 blocks stacked. The h: 4 + 7 + 5 = all 16 blocks stacked. The histogram shows a busy middle. 'Low numbers,' Pimm? Really?
map.Min 12, Q1 15, median 21, Q3 30, max 35: Min 12, Q1 15, median 21, Q3 30, max 35. IQR 15. The official chart's box was nowhere near this. Crooked confirmed.
map.Three cuts true — now the IQR: subtract: Three cuts are right. Now the IQR: subtract Q1 from Q3.
map.At least one cut missed. Median first (t: At least one cut missed. Median first (the 4th value). Then the middle of each half.
60 ÷ 5 = 12 batches, 94.5 ÷ 7 = 13.5 L. Every stack level. Every share fair. To the hearing!
map.Leveling ① first: total all five days, t: Leveling ① first: add all five days, then split equally among 5.
map.Leveling ② holds: 94.5 ÷ 7. Try splittin: Leveling ② holds: 94.5 ÷ 7. Try splitting 94.5 into 70 + 24.5.
map.Lock 1 holds. Sum all five days — the to: Lock 1 holds. Add all five days. The total ends in 7. Then divide by 5.
map.Lock 2 holds. Five ordered values — the: Lock 2 holds. Five values in order. The median is the 3rd one.
map.Lock 3 holds. Which number is close to t: Lock 3 holds. Which number is close to the days Rosa REALLY had: 65.4 or your median?
map.Lock 4 holds. The reason must mention wh: Lock 4 holds. The reason must say what the outlier DOES to the mean. Not which number is bigger. Not a rule that 'always' works.
map.ALL LOCKS OPEN. Mean 65.4 was parade-day: ALL LOCKS OPEN. Mean 65.4 was parade-day glitter. Median 45 is the truth. Permit RESTORED. The census is honest again!
Yes! Now go back and open that gate.
map.Walk the steps above again — you've got: Walk the steps above again. You can do it.
